title: Hepatobiliary & Pancreatic Disorders: Cirrhosis, Cholangitis & Acute Pancreatitis
html:
Liver, bile-duct, and pancreatic disorders often overlap: a client with abdominal pain may also have infection, bleeding, fluid shifts, or organ failure. The RN's task is not to diagnose from one laboratory value; it is to recognize a changing pattern, support stabilization, and communicate when source control or specialist treatment cannot wait. This final Adult Health / Med-Surg I lesson links decompensated cirrhosis, biliary infection, and acute pancreatitis.

Learning goals

  • Recognize ascites complications, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), encephalopathy, kidney injury, and variceal hemorrhage.
  • Differentiate biliary colic or cholecystitis from suspected acute cholangitis with systemic illness.
  • Monitor acute pancreatitis severity and support individualized fluids, analgesia, and early nutrition.
  • Prioritize urgent escalation, ordered treatment, and reassessment using clinical judgment.

Decompensated cirrhosis: watch the complications

Cirrhosis may remain compensated for years. Ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and portal-hypertensive GI bleeding signal decompensation. Assess abdominal distension, edema, weight trend, breathing, urine output, blood pressure, mentation, stool or emesis blood, jaundice, medication exposure, and the patient's usual baseline. Laboratory tests may include blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, bilirubin, albumin, and coagulation studies, but no isolated result replaces a bedside perfusion assessment. A person with cirrhosis can be visibly fluid overloaded yet have low effective arterial circulating volume and worsening kidney perfusion; avoid assuming that edema makes hypotension or oliguria harmless.

For ascites, follow the individualized sodium, diuretic, fluid, daily-weight, and intake-output plan. Monitor for dizziness, low blood pressure, falling urine output, rising creatinine, or potassium and sodium abnormalities during treatment. Therapeutic large-volume paracentesis may require ordered albumin replacement and postprocedure perfusion assessment. New or worsening ascites, hospitalization with cirrhosis and ascites, abdominal pain, fever, unexplained encephalopathy, or kidney deterioration should prompt timely evaluation for SBP, commonly by diagnostic paracentesis. SBP can occur without dramatic fever or tenderness; do not dismiss a subtle change. An ascitic-fluid polymorphonuclear neutrophil count of at least 250 cells/mm³ supports SBP treatment even if culture is negative. Help obtain ordered specimens promptly, then give prescribed antimicrobials and albumin when indicated; trend vitals, renal function, and response.

Hepatic encephalopathy can range from sleep-pattern or attention change to confusion and coma. Check airway protection and safety when consciousness declines, and search with the team for triggers such as infection, GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration, electrolyte problems, sedatives, or kidney injury. Lactulose is often titrated to the prescribed stool and clinical response; record stool count and consistency, mentation, hydration, and electrolytes. Excess diarrhea can worsen dehydration. Rifaximin may be added in selected cases. An ammonia result alone should not substitute for a clinical neurologic assessment or delay investigation of other causes of altered mental status.

Hematemesis or melena in a client with cirrhosis raises concern for variceal bleeding. Assess airway, hemodynamics, mental status, and ongoing blood loss; activate the appropriate urgent response. Support ordered IV access, blood testing and resuscitation, prescribed vasoactive therapy and antibiotic prophylaxis, and urgent endoscopic evaluation. Do not wait for a low first hemoglobin if shock signs are present. Continue checking for rebleeding, aspiration, encephalopathy, and kidney injury after hemostasis.

Biliary disease: infection plus obstruction is an emergency

Gallstones may cause episodic right-upper-quadrant pain; acute cholecystitis usually adds persistent inflammation and often fever or focal tenderness. Acute cholangitis is infection of an obstructed biliary system. Fever, right-upper-quadrant pain, and jaundice form the classic triad, but not every client has all three. Hypotension, confusion, rigors, or organ dysfunction suggest severe infection and possible sepsis. Trend temperature, blood pressure, mental status, urine output, bilirubin and liver tests, lactate when ordered, and imaging findings. Report suspected cholangitis promptly; support ordered cultures, IV fluids balanced against comorbidity, antibiotics, and GI or surgical consultation. Antibiotics alone may not adequately treat an obstructed infected duct. Biliary drainage, commonly by ERCP, is the source-control decision for the team; arrange timely preparation and monitor after the procedure for bleeding, pancreatitis, or persistent sepsis.

Acute pancreatitis: treat the patient, not only the lipase

Acute pancreatitis commonly presents with persistent upper-abdominal pain, often radiating to the back, with nausea or vomiting. Causes include gallstones and alcohol, among others. Diagnosis generally uses two of three features: characteristic pain, pancreatic enzymes at least three times the upper limit of normal, or compatible imaging. A higher lipase by itself does not grade severity. Repeatedly assess pain, vital signs, oxygenation, mental status, urine output, hydration, abdominal findings, blood urea nitrogen, hematocrit, creatinine, and electrolytes. Persistent organ failure, hypoxemia, shock, or kidney injury signals more severe disease and requires escalation.

Support ordered isotonic IV fluids early, but reassess often for perfusion and overload, particularly in heart or kidney disease; indiscriminate large-volume infusion is not a safety goal. Provide ordered analgesia and antiemetics, and monitor respiratory effects of opioids. In mild disease, resume oral low-fat food early as tolerated rather than keeping every patient NPO until enzymes normalize. For patients unable to eat with moderately severe or severe disease, the team may choose enteral feeding. Routine prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated for sterile pancreatic inflammation or necrosis; treat a proven or suspected infection such as cholangitis according to orders. Gallstone pancreatitis with concurrent cholangitis needs urgent biliary evaluation and usually ERCP, whereas uncomplicated gallstone pancreatitis does not automatically require urgent ERCP.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Compare pain, fever, jaundice, bleeding, mentation, blood pressure, oxygenation, weight, and urine output with baseline.
  2. Analyze cues: Ask whether the pattern fits ascites or SBP, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, biliary obstruction with infection, or pancreatitis with organ injury; more than one process may coexist.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Airway compromise, shock, active hemorrhage, sepsis or cholangitis, and worsening kidney or respiratory function take precedence.
  4. Generate solutions: Prepare ordered labs, cultures, paracentesis, imaging, resuscitation, medicines, specialist evaluation, and possible endoscopic source control.
  5. Take action: Escalate instability immediately, administer prescribed treatment, use aspiration and fall precautions when appropriate, and document accurate intake, output, stool, and reassessment trends.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Look for improving perfusion, mentation, urine output, oxygenation, pain, fever, bleeding, and ability to tolerate nutrition; report new decline despite treatment.

Clinical example

A client with cirrhosis and ascites becomes newly confused, hypotensive, and oliguric without a clear fever. The RN does not attribute the change to ammonia alone. After assessing airway and perfusion, the RN initiates the urgent-response pathway, reports possible infection or bleeding, prepares ordered diagnostic paracentesis and laboratory work, and supports timely treatment. If the same client also has jaundice and right-upper-quadrant pain, biliary infection remains in the differential and may need separate source control.
